title: Neurophysiological and psychological effects of color and ceiling height in learning spaces
research_question:
1. How do different color properties affect students' neurophysiological and psychological responses?
2. What is the effect of ceiling height variations on students' neuro-physiological and psychological responses?
3. How do neurophysiological responses correlate with subjective spatial perceptions and satisfaction in learning spaces?

participants.description: Forty Korean undergraduate students (14 males, 26 females; age range: 20-26 years, M = 22.93, SD = 1.31) from a university in South Korea. EEG data from 37 participants were included in the final analysis.
participants.recruitment: on-campus bulletin boards and online postings

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Immersive virtual learning environments modeled in 3D (SketchUp, Enscape) reflecting a studio-based classroom (16m L x 8m W). Featured one windowed wall, white desks, gray chairs, dark gray floor, white ceiling. Manipulated variables: six color schemes (red, green, blue hues x high-value low-chroma (HVLC) and low-value high-chroma (LVHC)) and four ceiling heights (3, 4, 5, 6 m). Each virtual environment presented for 2 min.

mechanisms: Color influences neurophysiological and psychological responses through sensory perception and emotional responses, with blue tones promoting relaxation and comfort, and deeper tones (LVHC) being less visually stimulating and more calming.

Ceiling height affects spatial perception and vestibular processing, influencing feelings of openness, spaciousness, and familiarity, which in turn modulate psychological comfort and neural relaxation.
Alpha power in parieto-occipital regions indicates reduced cortical activation in response to non-demanding visual stimuli, suggesting visual comfort and relaxation.
Frontal lobe activity (reduced alpha power) is associated with higher-order cognitive processing, suggesting reduced cognitive load.
implementation_implications: Blue color schemes, regardless of value and chroma, are recommended for learning environments to support emotional comfort.
A ceiling height of 4 to 5 meters may offer a balanced condition for both neural relaxation and emotional comfort in learning spaces.
Spatial proportion and perception should be considered when designing ceiling heights, rather than treating height as an isolated dimension.
Design strategies should prioritize users' psychological well-being in studio-based, collaborative, and project-oriented educational contexts.

limitations: Reliance on VR-based simulations may lack sensory and contextual richness of real-world settings (e.g., ambient temperature, acoustics, tactile sensations).
Experimental task was limited to passive observation, not fully capturing the complexity and dynamics of student activities.
Study focused on color and ceiling height as isolated variables, not their interaction with other environmental elements (e.g., lighting, furniture, acoustics).
Lack of cross-group comparisons for color and ceiling height.
Relatively short exposure duration to stimuli.
Potential variability in neurophysiological responses attributable to individual differences; future studies could benefit from larger sample sizes and controls for personal characteristics.
Lack of additional physiological metrics (e.g., heart rate variability, galvanic skin response) to offer a more comprehensive understanding of relaxation and stress.
